lead: The principle of increase of entropy tells you whether a process can happen. An engineer needs more: how much entropy a compressor, a turbine, a throttle valve or a heat exchanger generates, so that the losses can be ranked and priced. This chapter writes entropy as a balance, like mass and energy: entropy enters and leaves with heat and with flowing mass, and irreversibility generates more inside. It ends with the molecular picture behind entropy, S = k ln W, and shows that it gives the same number as the heat-over-temperature definition.
prereq: You need: the principle of increase of entropy, the entropy change of an ideal gas, and the steady flow energy equation from the first-law topics.

sections.h3: The entropy balance: transfer plus generation

blocks.text: Entropy crosses a boundary in only two ways: with heat and with flowing mass. Work carries no entropy. Inside the boundary, friction, mixing, unrestrained expansion and heat flow across a finite temperature difference create entropy, and nothing can destroy it. For a closed system going from state 1 to state 2:

blocks.where: S₂ − S₁ is the change in the system’s entropy, in kJ/K; Qⱼ is a heat transfer in kJ (positive into the system) that crosses the boundary where the boundary temperature is Tⱼ in K; Qⱼ/Tⱼ is the entropy that heat carries; S<sub>gen</sub> ≥ 0 is the entropy generated inside, zero only for an internally reversible process.

blocks.text: For an isolated system no heat and no mass cross, so S₂ − S₁ = S<sub>gen</sub> ≥ 0: the principle of increase of entropy is the special case of this balance.

sections.h3: Control volumes: the rate form and steady flow

blocks.text: A control volume also has streams of mass, and each kilogram brings its specific entropy s with it. Written per second:

dScv/dt = Σ Q̇ⱼ/Tⱼ + Σ ṁᵢsᵢ − Σ ṁₑsₑ + Ṡgen
dScv/dt is the rate of change of entropy inside, in kW/K; Q̇ⱼ is a heat rate in kW crossing where the boundary is at Tⱼ; ṁᵢ and ṁₑ are the mass flow rates in kg/s at each inlet and exit; sᵢ and sₑ are the specific entropies there in kJ/(kg·K); Ṡgen ≥ 0 is the rate of entropy generation in kW/K.
In steady flow nothing inside changes, so dS<sub>cv</sub>/dt = 0. With one inlet 1, one exit 2 and a single mass flow ṁ:

items: Adiabatic device (an insulated turbine, compressor, nozzle or throttle): Q̇ = 0, so s₂ ≥ s₁. The exit entropy equals the inlet entropy only for the reversible, isentropic device.
Device that loses heat to surroundings at T₀: the heat term is −Q̇out/T₀, so the stream may even leave with less entropy than it brought, provided the heat carries enough away.
Throttle valve on an ideal gas: h₂ = h₁, so T₂ = T₁ and Ṡgen = ṁR ln(p₁/p₂). All of it is generation; pressure is lost and nothing is gained.

blocks.text: Each kW/K generated costs T₀Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> kW of work, where T₀ is the temperature of the surroundings in K (the Gouy-Stodola relation). Adding these lost-work figures over a plant shows which component to fix first: the second-law analysis that the topic of available energy and exergy carries further.
A macrostate is what we measure: p, V, T. A microstate is one exact arrangement of every molecule’s position and energy that gives that macrostate. Boltzmann linked the two:

blocks.where: k = 1.381 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J/K is Boltzmann’s constant, the gas constant per molecule (R̄ divided by Avogadro’s number); W is the number of microstates that give the same macrostate. More ways of arranging the molecules means more entropy.

blocks.text: Let a gas double its volume freely, as in the free-expansion example of reversible and irreversible processes. Each of the N molecules now has twice the room, so W grows by a factor of 2N and ΔS = k ln 2N = Nk ln 2. For 0.5 kg of air, N = (0.5/28.97) kmol × 6.022 × 1026 per kmol = 1.04 × 1025 molecules, and Nk = 0.1435 kJ/K, which is exactly mR = 0.5 × 0.287. So ΔS = 0.1435 × 0.6931 = 0.0995 kJ/K, the same as mR ln 2 from the gas formula.

Heat opens more energy arrangements to the molecules, and the same heat added at a low temperature, where few were open, raises W by a larger factor: that is why dS = δQ<sub>rev</sub>/T has T at the bottom. Work moves the molecules together and adds no arrangements, so it carries no entropy.

spec.aria: A compressor inside a dashed control volume: air enters at 0.5 kg/s, 100 kPa and 300 K and leaves at 400 kPa and 480 K; 95 kW of power goes in and 4.55 kW of heat leaves to air at 300 K. An entropy account below lists 0.0372 kW/K carried out by the air, 0.0152 kW/K carried by the heat and 0.0524 kW/K generated.

examples.question: Air flows steadily through a compressor at 0.5 kg/s. It enters at 100 kPa and 300 K and leaves at 400 kPa and 480 K. The power input is 95 kW, and the casing loses heat to the surroundings at 300 K. Take c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K) and R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), and neglect kinetic and potential energy. Find (a) the heat lost, (b) the entropy change of the air per kg, (c) the rate of entropy generation, (d) the lost work, and (e) the power an isentropic compressor would need between the same pressures.
steps: (a) Steady flow energy equation: the air gains ṁc<sub>p</sub>(T₂ − T₁) = 0.5 × 1.005 × (480 − 300) = 90.45 kW. The power in is 95 kW, so heat lost Q̇<sub>out</sub> = 95 − 90.45 = 4.55 kW.
Entropy carried out by the air: ṁΔs = 0.5 × 0.0745 = 0.0372 kW/K.
Heat term: the heat leaves where the boundary is at T₀ = 300 K, so Σ Q̇/T = −4.55/300 = −0.0152 kW/K.
(c) Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> = ṁ(s₂ − s₁) − Σ Q̇/T = 0.0372 − (−0.0152) = 0.0524 kW/K. It is positive, so the process is possible and irreversible.

(e) Isentropic exit temperature: T₂ₛ = T₁(p₂/p₁)<sup>R/cp</sup> = 300 × 4<sup>0.2856</sup> = 300 × 1.4857 = 445.7 K. Isentropic power = 0.5 × 1.005 × (445.7 − 300) = 73.2 kW, so the isentropic efficiency is 73.2/95 = 0.77.
examples.answer: Heat lost 4.55 kW; Δs = +0.0745 kJ/(kg·K); Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> = 0.0524 kW/K; lost work 15.7 kW; an isentropic compressor would need 73.2 kW, an isentropic efficiency of 0.77.

traps: Work carries no entropy. Adding a Ẇ/T term to the balance is a common slip; there is no such term.
Each heat term uses the boundary temperature where the heat crosses, with its sign: heat lost gives −Q̇/T₀. Dropping it in the worked example gives Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> = 0.0372 instead of 0.0524 kW/K.
s₂ > s₁ alone does not prove irreversibility when heat crosses the boundary, and s₂ < s₁ is allowed when enough heat leaves. Only Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> ≥ 0 is the test.
Lost work T₀Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> is not the same as actual minus isentropic power: 15.7 kW against 95 − 73.2 = 21.8 kW in the example, because the hotter exit air still carries some useful energy.
In S = k ln W, k is per molecule; for a bulk gas Nk = mR.

quiz.q: Write the steady-flow entropy balance for a device with one inlet and one exit, and name each term.
quiz.a: Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> = ṁ(s₂ − s₁) − Σ Q̇ⱼ/Tⱼ ≥ 0: ṁ is the mass flow in kg/s, s₁ and s₂ the inlet and exit specific entropies, Q̇ⱼ each heat rate crossing where the boundary is at Tⱼ, and Ṡ<sub>gen</sub> the entropy generated, in kW/K.

quiz.q: State Boltzmann’s relation for entropy and define its symbols.
quiz.a: S = k ln W, where k = 1.381 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J/K is Boltzmann’s constant and W is the number of microstates (molecular arrangements) that give the same macrostate.

quiz.q: Why does heat carry entropy across a boundary while work does not?
quiz.a: Heat spreads energy among the molecules’ random motions and opens more arrangements, so it carries entropy Q/T. Work is an ordered transfer, like raising a weight, that moves molecules together and adds no arrangements, so it carries none.

quiz.q: Air is throttled steadily from 500 kPa to 100 kPa through an insulated valve. Treating it as an ideal gas with R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), find the entropy generated per kg.
quiz.a: For a throttle h₂ = h₁, so T₂ = T₁ for an ideal gas. Δs = −R ln(p₂/p₁) = 0.287 ln 5 = 0.287 × 1.6094 = 0.4619 kJ/(kg·K). The valve is adiabatic, so s<sub>gen</sub> = 0.4619 kJ/(kg·K).

quiz.q: An insulated air turbine takes air at 600 K and 500 kPa and exhausts it at 400 K and 100 kPa. With c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 and R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), find s₂ − s₁ and say whether the process is possible.
quiz.a: s₂ − s₁ = 1.005 ln(400/600) − 0.287 ln(100/500) = −0.4075 + 0.4619 = +0.0544 kJ/(kg·K). The turbine is adiabatic, so this is the entropy generated; it is positive, so the process is possible and irreversible.

quiz.q: A claim: an insulated device with no work input takes air at 300 K and 100 kPa and delivers it at 300 K and 200 kPa. Test it with the entropy balance.
quiz.a: Δs = c<sub>p</sub> ln 1 − 0.287 ln 2 = −0.1989 kJ/(kg·K). With Q̇ = 0, s<sub>gen</sub> = Δs = −0.1989 < 0, which the second law forbids. The device is impossible (the first law is satisfied, since h is unchanged and no work crosses).

quiz.q: Show that S = k ln W gives the same entropy rise as mR ln(V₂/V₁) when an ideal gas doubles its volume.
quiz.a: Each of N molecules has twice the volume, so W rises by 2<sup>N</sup> and ΔS = Nk ln 2. Since N = (m/M)N<sub>A</sub> and k = R̄/N<sub>A</sub>, Nk = mR̄/M = mR. So ΔS = mR ln 2, the macroscopic result.

beyond: Not for the exam. Entropy generation minimisation sizes heat exchangers and ducts by trading the entropy made by fluid friction against the entropy made by temperature differences. In a steam plant audit the boiler usually tops the list of T₀Ṡ<sub>gen</sub>. The Gibbs formula S = −k Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ extends Boltzmann’s relation and has the same form as Shannon’s information entropy. Search next for entropy generation minimisation and the Gouy-Stodola theorem.
